body.en: Trigonometry studies the relationships between angles and sides of triangles. Right-triangle definitions extend to all real angles via the unit circle, giving the six trigonometric functions, laws of sines and cosines, and the area formula.

problem.en: A triangle has sides \(a=7, b=9, c=5\). Find angle \(B\).

solution.en:
\(b\sin A=8\sin30°=4.\) Since \(b\sin A=4 < a=6 < b=8\): two triangles possible.

\(\sin B=\dfrac{b\sin A}{a}=\dfrac{8(0.5)}{6}=\dfrac{2}{3}.\quad B_1=\arcsin(2/3)\approx41.8°\) or \(B_2=180°-41.8°=138.2°.\)

Triangle 1: \(B_1\approx41.8°,\;C_1\approx108.2°.\) Triangle 2: \(B_2\approx138.2°,\;C_2\approx11.8°.\) Both valid since all angles positive and sum to 180°.

label.en: ▲ Pre-Calculus Traps & Commandments — Trigonometry & Triangle Laws

body.en:
• Radian vs. Degree Mode: Always verify calculator mode before computing. Arc length \(s = r\theta\) and sector area \(A = \frac{1}{2}r^2\theta\) strictly require \(\theta\) in radians.
  • Ambiguous SSA Case: When using the Law of Sines with SSA, check the altitude \(h = b\sin A\). If \(h < a < b\), two distinct valid triangles exist: \(B_1 = \arcsin(b\sin A / a)\) (acute) and \(B_2 = 180° - B_1\) (obtuse), provided \(A + B_2 < 180°\).
  • Law of Cosines Angle Selection: In SSS triangles, solve for the largest angle first (opposite the longest side) using the Law of Cosines. Because \(\arccos\) outputs values across \([0°, 180°]\), it automatically identifies obtuse angles, avoiding the ambiguity of \(\arcsin\).
  • Area Formulas: Use \(K = \frac{1}{2}ab\sin C\) when two sides and the included angle are known (SAS). Use Heron's formula \(K = \sqrt{s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)}\) with semi-perimeter \(s = (a+b+c)/2\) when all three sides are known (SSS).

question.en: In \(\triangle ABC\), \(a = 8\), \(b = 11\), and \(A = 35°\). Determine the number of possible triangles and find the measure of angle \(B\) for all valid cases to the nearest tenth of a degree.

solution.en:
Calculate the altitude \(h = b\sin A = 11\sin 35° \approx 11(0.5736) = 6.31\).

Since \(h < a < b\) (\(6.31 < 8 < 11\)), there are two possible triangles.

By the Law of Sines: \[\sin B = \frac{b\sin A}{a} = \frac{6.31}{8} \approx 0.7887.\]

First solution (acute): \(B_1 = \arcsin(0.7887) \approx 52.1°\).

Second solution (obtuse): \(B_2 = 180° - 52.1° = 127.9°\).

Check validity: \(A + B_2 = 35° + 127.9° = 162.9° < 180°\), which allows \(C_2 = 17.1° > 0\). Both \(B_1 \approx 52.1°\) and \(B_2 \approx 127.9°\) are valid.

question.en: A surveyor measures distances from an observation point \(C\) to two landmarks \(A\) and \(B\): \(AC = 140\text{ m}\) and \(BC = 210\text{ m}\), with included angle \(\angle ACB = 78°\). Find the distance \(AB\) between the landmarks to the nearest tenth of a meter, and compute the area of \(\triangle ABC\) to the nearest square meter.
